item.title: Refining the lighting and the leather
item.content:
The first test renders work, but the shadows have hard, ugly edges and the scene is greyer than the photos of the real chair. In this part you'll soften the shadows by changing the size of the lights, turn the rim light into a spotlight, add a sun to brighten the whole scene, make the floor matte, and find a light that was still rendering although it was hidden. Then you'll give the leather a roughness map and a normal map so it stops looking like plastic. You'll need the lit scene from the previous part and your textured chair. The video uses Blender 2.83.

Soften the shadows

  1. Look through the camera and find the hard shadows. 0:00 Click the camera icon beside the viewport to look through the render camera. The ugly shadowing you see can be fixed by moving the lights or the camera, or by changing the size of the lights.

  2. Scale the lights up for softer shadows. 0:30 The smaller a light source is, the harder the edge of its shadow. Select a light and press S to scale it up, and the shadow it makes becomes much softer.

  3. Place each light for what it lights. 1:00 The video makes the rim light smaller, raises it and moves it to the side to lay a little light across the top of the chair. Where you put a light depends on what you're trying to light: to catch a highlight in one place, or to lay light across the top.

  4. Turn the rim light into a spotlight. 1:30 With the light selected, choose Spot in its light settings. A spot gives you a cone of light; change the cone's size with Size under Spot Shape 1:53 (not the light's own Size above it), and angle it. Then raise its Power 2:04: 200 W is a little low, and after hiding the light for a moment with its eye icon in the Outliner, the video tries 1000 W 2:52.

  5. Check the result. 2:57 Look through the camera in rendered view again. Overall the shadows are cleaner, without the hard edges from before.

Brighten the scene with a sun

  1. Compare with the reference photos. 3:10 In the side and front reference photos of the real chair, the background is much brighter. The scene has a lot of grey and needs more light overall, and because the lights cover only a small area, very little reaches the background.

  2. Add a sun. 3:57 There are all sorts of ways to light the background; the video adds a Sun light. A sun is a directional light: it casts light everywhere, evenly, in one direction. Press R to rotate it and you'll see long shadows; here it should point straight down, so its default rotation is good. The scene is much brighter 4:29. Every light you add makes the render take longer, so keep that in mind.

  3. Keep the area lights. 4:40 Turn the area lights off and the chair is still really dark, so you need them as well as the sun.

  4. Soften the sun's shadow. 4:52 The sun makes a really dark, awful shadow under the chair. Unchecking Cast Shadow in its light settings removes the shadow entirely 5:18, but the sun then overpowers the other lights' shadows too, so check it again. Instead, turn the sun's Angle way up 5:42: the sun still points down, but its shadow is much softer. The video also raises its Strength to 1.2 6:09.

Make the floor matte

  1. Give the floor a material. 6:18 Select the backdrop and open its material settings: it has no material of its own yet, so click New.

  2. Raise its roughness to 1. 6:39 In the Principled BSDF shader, Roughness controls the specularity: anywhere there's a bright spot is specular. Set Roughness to 1 to make the floor more even.

Find a stray light

  1. Make a quicker test render. 7:00 In the render settings, set Sampling › Render to 128 for now; you'll use more samples at the end. This is just to check the lighting. The render shows a hard shadow that wasn't visible before 7:29.

  2. Show the Outliner's render toggles. 7:44 In the Outliner, the arrow icon turns selecting on and off and the eye icon turns things on and off in the viewport, but there's also a render icon. Open the Outliner's Filter menu and turn on the camera icon under Restriction Toggles. The new column shows that the default light, hidden in the viewport, was still turned on for rendering: turn it off there 8:13. Even before the render finishes, the hard-edged shadow is gone 8:24. Be careful with this: hiding something in the viewport doesn't keep it out of the render.

Light the back of the chair

  1. Undo what made the lighting flat. 8:42 With everything this bright, the lighting is pretty flat, so the video undoes some changes and scales the lights back down.

  2. Aim the spotlight in Material Preview. 9:10 Switch the viewport to Material Preview (once called LookDev, a texture-shading view) to move the spotlight more easily. The back of the chair isn't getting any light, so angle the spotlight down until it covers that surface 9:54, taking care not to cast shadows. Check it through the render camera, where you might not see the light at all, and make it more top-down if you need to 10:08.

  3. Brighten the key light. 10:29 The fill light at 80 W is pretty good. Raise the key light to 700 W 10:39.

  4. Render at 250 samples. 10:48 In the render settings, set Render sampling to 250: for this scene, more doesn't give much better results. Render. The result is a pretty good quality render 11:16: there's specularity on the rounded part of the seat and nice highlights on parts of the chair. Without a bevel on those edges (depending on your model) you might not see these highlights, and they're what really sells a render like this.

  5. Keep this render. 11:56 Leave it in Slot 2 and choose Slot 3, so the next render goes there.

Make the leather look like leather

  1. Open the seat's material in the Shading workspace. 12:08 The leather looks more like plastic. Go to the Shading workspace and select the seat cushion. The leather image you added earlier through the material settings is connected to the Base Color; here you can see it as nodes, bring in more images and plug them into other parts of the shader.

  2. Get the matching maps. 12:56 The video's leather texture came from CC0 Textures (cc0textures.com). Searching for "leather" finds the same texture, and its download, a folder named Leather014_2K-JPG, holds four images: the colour image you've already applied, and displacement, normal and roughness maps, each named in the file name 13:16. This part uses the normal and roughness maps; displacement is a bit more advanced.

  3. Bring the images into the Shader Editor. 13:39 Drag each image into the Shader Editor and it becomes an Image Texture node. To add one by hand, use Add and search for "image". Arrange the nodes so you stay organized.

  4. Connect the roughness map. 14:18 Plug the roughness image's Color into the shader's Roughness. A roughness map isn't really colour information: it uses black and white to map where the surface is rough.

  5. Connect the normal map through a Normal Map node. 14:23 Plugging the normal image straight into Normal isn't right: a normal map isn't colour information either. It tells the shader where the surface has physical, topological changes. Add a Normal Map node 15:05, plug the image's Color into its Color and its Normal into the shader's Normal. Then set the normal image's Color Space to Non-Color instead of sRGB, because it won't work properly otherwise, and in the Normal Map node choose your object's UV map 15:29.

  6. Check it and lower the strength. 15:37 Now there's a sheen that follows the ridges of the leather, and it looks bumpy, almost sculpted; unplug the normal map to see that it's what makes the bumps. If it's too bumpy, lower the Normal Map node's Strength slowly (hold Shift while dragging) until it just starts to read 16:10. Check it in rendered view 16:28.

  7. Add contrast to the roughness with a ColorRamp. 16:37 If you want, add contrast to the roughness: press Shift A, search for a ColorRamp node and drop it between the roughness image and the shader. A ColorRamp applies a gradient to the colour coming in, so it can assign new values to the image; bring its black and white stops closer together to increase the contrast. To see what's happening, plug it into Base Color for a moment and use Material Preview 17:19, and don't overdo it. When the video tries it, the leather looks a little wet, so it backs the white stop off a little 17:57. You might not need to adjust yours at all.

  8. Do the same for the back cushion. 18:35 Select the back cushion and connect the same roughness and normal images to its material, with a Normal Map node set to your UVs 19:10. A strength of 1 is a little too strong for the video; it uses something like 0.3, but make your own choice 19:31.

  9. Render and compare. 19:39 The key light's highlight on the curve now has a bit more detail: it doesn't look so flat, it spreads out through the normal map's details, and the reflections and specularity are broken up over the texture instead of solid. That adds realism. Render into Slot 3, then zoom in and switch between slots 3 and 2 20:28: without the maps, the detail disappears. Just adding those two textures and a little configuration makes the chair look significantly more real.

  10. Decide whether the wood needs maps too. 21:04 You could do the same for the wood. Here it's highly polished wood on what is probably a very expensive, well-crafted object, so the video leaves it as it is. Older wood would have a normal map that highlights its ridges and imperfections, so if your texture is different, go ahead and add one.

Wrap-up

Bigger lights give softer shadows, a sun brightens the whole scene, and the Outliner's render toggles show what will really appear in the render. A roughness map and a normal map, each connected the right way, turn a flat colour into leather that catches the light. With that, the render is finished; the last part takes it into Photoshop.
